strengths: EA-KD is a simple, practical modification that combines teacher and student entropy to weight distillation losses. It requires no auxiliary network and applies to both logit and feature distillation, making it relevant to efficient computer vision.

The experimental coverage is substantial. Table 2 reports improvements in 46 of 49 method–architecture combinations, averaging 0.56 percentage points. Improvements extend to ImageNet (+0.76 points over KD), transformer teachers, and COCO detection (+0.81 and +1.68 AP over KD). These results support practical usefulness beyond a single configuration.

The manuscript includes useful entropy-weighting, temperature, and component ablations, alongside comparisons with related adaptive methods. The supplementary WTTM comparison addresses particularly relevant prior work.

The core formulation is clearly presented, datasets and underlying methods are generally attributed appropriately, and a code repository is linked. Supplementary Tables C4–C5 provide variability across repeated runs for the proposed variants, improving the evidence beyond reporting single results.
weaknesses: The principal concern is that sample prioritization is confounded with overall distillation strength. Equations (12)–(14) use weights without normalizing their mean, so the effective KD coefficient changes with temperature, class count, and student confidence. Section 4.1 even reduces the MLD+LS coefficient from 9 to 4. A tuned scalar-weight baseline, a control matching the average weight over training, and mean-normalized weighting are needed to establish that the gains arise from selecting informative samples. This unresolved control is the main reason for a borderline-reject assessment.

The distinct contribution of student-dependent adaptation is only modestly supported. WTTM already emphasizes uncertain teacher predictions, as acknowledged in Appendix A.1. In Table 9, adding the proposed interaction to teacher-only weighting improves KD, MLD, and MLD+LS by just 0.32, 0.18, and 0.08 points, respectively, and slightly reduces FCFD accuracy. This ablation covers only one teacher–student pair, leaving the general advantage of the new adaptive component uncertain.

The interpretation of entropy as learning value is stronger than the supporting analysis. Equations (5)–(7) correctly describe a uniformly initialized student, but smaller KL divergence for an uncertain teacher does not establish harmful optimization bias. When both distributions are uniform, the loss and its gradient are already zero; weighting cannot resolve that limiting example. Likewise, t-SNE cluster positions do not establish actual decision boundaries. High entropy may also reflect teacher error or ambiguity, which the analysis does not separate from useful transferable knowledge.

The strongest-baseline comparisons need better uncertainty control. Appendix C explains that baseline means are taken from prior reports, while deviations are supplied primarily for EA variants. Thus, small improvements cannot be assessed through matched repeated runs. In Table A1, EA-TTM exceeds WTTM by only 0.03–0.19 points against appreciable reported variability, which does not convincingly establish the claimed superiority of dynamic weighting. A minor reporting inconsistency also needs correction: Table 9 gives EA-FCFD as 77.44, whereas Tables 2 and C4 report 77.50 for the same pair.

Important implementation choices remain unspecified. The manuscript does not state whether gradients propagate through student entropy; doing so introduces an additional entropy-gradient term beyond reweighting the KD gradient. The aggregation of detection predictions into sample weights and of token entropies into sequence weights is also insufficiently defined. These details materially affect reproduction of the proposed extensions.
